paragraphs: We have seen that an uncontrollable power over elections to the federal government could not safely be committed to the State legislatures. Let us now see what the danger would be on the other side, that is, from trusting the Union itself with the ultimate right to regulate its own elections. It is not claimed that this right would ever be used to exclude any State from its share in the representation. The interest of all would, in this respect at least, be the security of all. But it is alleged that the right might be used to promote the election of some favorite class of men to the exclusion of others, by confining the places of election to particular districts and making it impracticable for the citizens at large to take part in the choice. Of all fanciful suppositions, this seems the most fanciful. On the one hand, no rational calculation of probabilities would lead us to imagine that the disposition implied by so violent and extraordinary a course could ever find its way into the national councils. On the other, we may conclude with certainty that if so improper a spirit ever did gain admission to them, it would show itself in a form altogether different and far more decisive.

The improbability of the attempt may be satisfactorily inferred from this single reflection: it could never be made without causing an immediate revolt of the great body of the people, headed and directed by the State governments. It is not difficult to conceive that this characteristic right of liberty may, in certain turbulent and factional seasons, be violated with respect to a particular class of citizens by a victorious and overbearing majority. But that so fundamental a privilege, in a country so situated and so enlightened, should be invaded to the injury of the great mass of the people by the deliberate policy of the government, without causing a popular revolution, is altogether inconceivable and incredible.

In addition to this general reflection, there are considerations of a more precise nature that forbid all apprehension on the subject. The dissimilarity in the elements that will compose the national government, and still more in the manner in which they will be brought into action in its various branches, must form a powerful obstacle to concert of views in any biased scheme of elections. There is enough diversity in the state of property and in the character, manners and habits of the people in the different parts of the Union to produce a material diversity of disposition among their representatives toward the different ranks and conditions in society. And though close intercourse under the same government will promote a gradual assimilation in some of these respects, there are causes, physical as well as moral, that may in a greater or lesser degree permanently nourish different inclinations in this regard. But the circumstance likely to have the greatest influence in the matter will be the dissimilar modes of constituting the separate component parts of the government. The House of Representatives is to be elected directly by the people, the Senate by the State legislatures, and the President by electors chosen for that purpose by the people. There would be little probability of a common interest to unite these different branches in a preference for any particular class of electors.

As to the Senate, it is impossible that any regulation of "time and manner," which is all that is proposed to be submitted to the national government with respect to that body, can affect the spirit that will direct the choice of its members. The collective view of the State legislatures can never be influenced by extraneous circumstances of that sort. This consideration alone ought to satisfy us that the feared discrimination would never be attempted. For what inducement could the Senate have to agree to a preference in which it would not itself be included? Or to what purpose would such a preference be established for one branch of the legislature if it could not be extended to the other? The composition of the one would in that case counteract that of the other. And we can never suppose that it would reach the appointments to the Senate unless we can at the same time suppose the voluntary cooperation of the State legislatures. If we make the latter supposition, it then becomes immaterial where the power in question is placed, whether in their hands or in those of the Union.

But what is to be the object of this arbitrary bias in the national councils? Is it to be exercised in discriminating between the different departments of industry, or between the different kinds of property, or between the different degrees of property? Will it lean in favor of the landed interest, or the moneyed interest, or the mercantile interest, or the manufacturing interest? Or, to use the fashionable language of the adversaries of the Constitution, will it court the elevation of "the wealthy and the well-born" to the exclusion and degradation of all the rest of the society?

If this bias is to be exerted in favor of those engaged in any particular description of industry or property, I presume it will readily be admitted that the competition for it will lie between landed men and merchants. And I do not hesitate to affirm that it is infinitely less likely that either of them should gain an ascendancy in the national councils than that one or the other should predominate in all the local councils. The inference is that conduct tending to give an undue preference to either is much less to be dreaded from the former than from the latter.

The individual States are devoted in varying degrees to agriculture and commerce. In most of them, if not all, agriculture is predominant. In a few, however, commerce nearly shares its empire, and in most it has a considerable share of influence. In proportion as either prevails, it will be carried into the national representation. And for the very reason that this representation will come from a greater variety of interests, in much more varied proportions, than are to be found in any single State, it will be much less apt to embrace either of them with decided partiality than the representation of any single State.

In a country consisting chiefly of cultivators of land, where the rules of equal representation prevail, the landed interest must on the whole preponderate in the government. As long as this interest prevails in most of the State legislatures, it must keep a corresponding superiority in the national Senate, which will generally be a faithful copy of the majorities of those assemblies. It cannot therefore be presumed that a sacrifice of the landed class to the mercantile class will ever be a favorite object of this branch of the federal legislature. In applying to the Senate in particular a general observation suggested by the situation of the country, I am guided by the consideration that the credulous devotees of State power cannot, on their own principles, suspect that the State legislatures would be warped from their duty by any external influence. But in reality the same situation must have the same effect, at least in the original composition of the federal House of Representatives: an improper bias toward the mercantile class is as little to be expected from this quarter as from the other.

Perhaps, in order to give the objection some countenance at any rate, it may be asked whether there is not danger of an opposite bias in the national government, which may dispose it to try to secure a monopoly of the federal administration for the landed class. Since there is little likelihood that the supposition of such a bias will have any terrors for those who would be directly injured by it, a labored answer to this question will be dispensed with. It will be sufficient to remark, first, that for the reasons given elsewhere, it is less likely that any decided partiality should prevail in the councils of the Union than in those of any of its members. Second, there would be no temptation to violate the Constitution in favor of the landed class, because that class would, in the natural course of things, enjoy as great a preponderance as it could desire. And third, men accustomed to investigating the sources of public prosperity on a large scale must be too well convinced of the usefulness of commerce to be inclined to inflict on it so deep a wound as would result from the complete exclusion from a share in managing public affairs of those who would best understand its interest. The importance of commerce, from the standpoint of revenue alone, must effectively guard it against the enmity of a body that would be continually pressed in its favor by the urgent calls of public necessity.

I am the more inclined to be brief in discussing the probability of a preference founded on a discrimination between the different kinds of industry and property because, as far as I understand the meaning of the objectors, they have a discrimination of another kind in view. They appear to have in mind, as the objects of the preference with which they try to alarm us, those whom they describe as "the wealthy and the well-born." These, it seems, are to be raised to an odious pre-eminence over the rest of their fellow citizens. At one time, however, their elevation is to be a necessary consequence of the smallness of the representative body; at another time it is to be brought about by depriving the people at large of the opportunity to exercise their right of suffrage in choosing that body.

But on what principle is the discrimination of the places of election to be made, in order to serve the purpose of the intended preference? Are "the wealthy and the well-born," as they are called, confined to particular spots in the individual States? Have they, by some miraculous instinct or foresight, set apart in each State a common place of residence? Are they to be found only in the towns or cities? Or are they, on the contrary, scattered over the face of the country, wherever greed or chance has happened to cast their own lot or that of their predecessors? If the latter is the case (as every intelligent man knows it to be,(1)) is it not evident that the policy of confining the places of election to particular districts would defeat its own aim, as well as being objectionable on every other account? The truth is that there is no way of securing to the rich the feared preference except by prescribing property qualifications for those who may elect or be elected. But this forms no part of the power to be conferred on the national government. Its authority would be expressly restricted to regulating the TIMES, the PLACES and the MANNER of elections. The qualifications of the persons who may choose or be chosen, as has been remarked on other occasions, are defined and fixed in the Constitution and cannot be altered by the legislature.

Let it nevertheless be admitted, for the sake of argument, that the suggested expedient might succeed. Let it at the same time be equally taken for granted that all the scruples which a sense of duty or fear of the danger of the experiment might inspire were overcome in the breasts of the national rulers. Still, I imagine, it will hardly be claimed that they could ever hope to carry such an enterprise into execution without a military force sufficient to overcome the resistance of the great body of the people. The improbability that a force equal to that object will exist has been discussed and demonstrated in different parts of these papers. But to show the futility of the objection under consideration in the strongest light, let it be conceded for a moment that such a force might exist, and let the national government be supposed to be in actual possession of it. What will be the conclusion? With a disposition to invade the essential rights of the community, and with the means of gratifying that disposition, is it likely that the persons actuated by it would amuse themselves with the ridiculous task of fabricating election laws to secure a preference for a favorite class of men? Would they not be likely to prefer a course better suited to their own immediate aggrandizement? Would they not rather boldly resolve to perpetuate themselves in office by one decisive act of usurpation, than trust to precarious expedients which, in spite of all the precautions that might accompany them, might end in the dismissal, disgrace and ruin of their authors? Would they not fear that citizens, no less tenacious than aware of their rights, would flock from the remote extremes of their States to the places of election, to overthrow their tyrants and to put in their place men who would be disposed to avenge the violated majesty of the people?
1. Particularly in the Southern States and in this State.
